an0445.user: Running Meta for my dental clinic, last 30 days. We pushed 4.5 lakh impressions, got 8,677 clicks so CTR is sitting at 1.9% which I'm honestly happy with. Targeting is broad, interest-based. But only 81 actual appointment bookings came through, conversion rate is 0.93%. The ads are clearly getting attention so why aren't people booking?
an0445.assistant:
Your CTR is fine — 1.9% means people like the ad. The problem is one step later: 8,677 clicks turned into 81 bookings, a 0.93% conversion rate. That gap is the whole story. You're buying broad, interest-based traffic, which means most of those clicks are curious scrollers, not someone with a toothache looking for a clinic this week. They tap because the ad is nice, then bounce because they weren't in the market. High clicks, low intent.

For a dental clinic, intent is everything. Somebody actively searching "root canal near me" or "dentist Indiranagar" is worth ten interest-based impressions. Right now you're optimising for clicks, and Meta is happily giving you the cheapest, lowest-intent ones it can find.

Stop chasing reach and tighten the audience: layer in local intent — people in your 5-7km radius, dental/health interest stacks, and run a parallel Google Search campaign on high-intent keywords where the buyer is already looking. Add negatives so you stop paying for tyre-kickers.

One caveat: 81 bookings is a usable but not huge sample. Once you tighten intent, judge it on cost-per-booking over a few hundred bookings, not CTR. CTR was never your problem.

an0446.user: Help me figure out what's wrong. No-code SaaS, email + Meta, last 30 days post-iOS. Meta dashboard says ROAS 4.1, Shopify last-click says 1.9 on ₹9L spend. Same period, same spend, two completely different numbers. Which one do I trust? I can't plan anything when my own dashboards are lying to me.
an0446.assistant:
Neither dashboard is lying — they're both telling a biased version of the truth, and the real number sits between them. Meta's 4.1 is modelled: it counts 7-day-click and view-through conversions and takes credit for sales it merely influenced. Shopify's 1.9 is last-click: it only credits the final tap and hands all the glory to "direct" and "google / organic" when someone saw your Meta ad, didn't click, and came back later. One over-counts, one under-counts. They will never agree, and waiting for them to is a trap.

Stop refereeing two scoreboards that are designed to disagree. Anchor on a number neither platform can spin: blended CAC. Take total spend across everything — ₹9L — and divide by actual new customers Shopify recorded that month. That's what it really cost you to buy a customer, and it doesn't care which dashboard claims the assist.

Manage to that blended number week over week. If blended CAC is below your contribution per new customer, you're winning regardless of whether Meta says 4.1 or Shopify says 1.9.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs channels, so once it's your north star, run the occasional geo-holdout or pause-test on Meta to see what actually moves — that's the only way to know Meta's true incremental contribution.

an0447.user: D2C home-care, blended Meta + Google. What's wrong here — last 8 weeks I scaled spend from ₹3.5L to ₹6.8L. CAC went ₹633 to ₹923, ROAS dropped 3.2 to 2.2. AOV ₹2050, gross margin 61%. I thought more budget = more sales but the efficiency is falling apart. Bad creative? Algorithm?
an0447.assistant:

That's the exact signature of saturation: your best, cheapest, highest-intent audiences are finite, and once you've harvested them the extra budget buys colder, more expensive reach. The pool didn't get bigger because you spent more — you just dug deeper into it.

The economics still work, for now: ₹2,050 × 61% − ₹923 = +₹328 contribution per order. So you're not bleeding. But the trend matters more than the snapshot — every extra rupee is converting worse, and if you keep pushing the same audiences, CAC keeps climbing until contribution goes negative.

The lever isn't more budget into the same pool — it's new demand. New audiences, new creative angles for cold prospects, and a genuine third channel (you're leaning on Meta + Google; what about WhatsApp re-engagement or Amazon for home-care?). Expand the pool, then scale.

Caveat: 8 weeks blends festive and non-festive demand and two platforms — split Meta vs Google before you decide which one actually saturated, because one of them might still have headroom.

an0448.user: Want your non-obvious read on this. Meesho Ads, skincare, last 6 weeks. CAC has gone from ₹697 to ₹1,401 — basically doubled. ROAS dropped 1.5 to 0.7. AOV ₹1,050, margin 43%. Frequency is 3.4. CTR is sliding. I haven't touched creatives or audience. Is Meesho's algorithm just getting worse for my category?
an0448.assistant:
It's not Meesho's algorithm — it's your creative, and the numbers spell it out cleanly. Same creatives, same audience, for six weeks; frequency now 3.4, meaning the average person has seen your ad more than three times; CTR sliding; CAC doubling ₹697 → ₹1,401. That's textbook creative fatigue. The audience hasn't gone bad — they've just seen the same thing too often and stopped reacting, so Meesho has to show it more (rising frequency) to fewer responsive people (falling CTR) at a higher cost (rising CAC).

And the economics have already flipped underwater: ₹1,050 × 43% − ₹1,401 = −₹950 per order. Every sale is now losing you nearly a thousand rupees. This isn't a "tune it" situation, it's a "the fuel ran out" situation.

The lever: refresh the creative with genuinely new angles — different hook, different problem, different format — not a colour swap on the same ad. Caveat: frequency 3.4 is the smoking gun, but confirm it's account-wide and not one fatigued ad set dragging the average — pause the worst offender first and watch CAC.

an0449.user: Skincare brand, just launched a Google Search campaign. 5 days in, spent ₹58K, got 19 conversions. I want a clean read — is my CAC good? Should I scale this or kill it? Trying not to waste money either way.
an0449.assistant:
Honest answer: you can't know yet, and any CAC I quote off this would be a guess dressed up as a number. 19 conversions over 5 days is far too small a sample — at that size, two good days or two dead days swing your "CAC" by 30-40%, so whatever figure you compute is mostly noise, not signal.

Don't scale and don't kill. Both are decisions, and you don't have enough data to make either one responsibly. Killing a campaign that was about to stabilise wastes the learning budget you already spent; scaling one that's actually inefficient burns real money.

Let it run to roughly 100 conversions, or a 2-3 week window, whichever comes first — that's the point where a CAC number stops being random and starts being real. Google's Search algorithm also needs that volume to exit its learning phase, so you're not just waiting on statistics, you're waiting on the system to settle.

Check back when you cross ~100 conversions. Then we'll have something worth diagnosing.

This is exactly how founders whipsaw their accounts: react to one noisy week, change creative and audience, then the next week reverts, and now you can't tell what your changes did versus what randomness did. You lose the ability to read your own data.

What would actually count as a signal: the same direction sustained for 3-4 weeks, or a single move big enough that random chance can't explain it — a 40-50% drop, not 16%. Until then, the data hasn't told you anything.

Sit on your hands one more week. If week three is also down, then we look — and at that point I'd start with whether frequency is climbing, not the agency.

an0454.user: Haircare D2C, email channel, last 30 days. AOV ₹850, margin 25%, CAC ₹414, ROAS 2.1, CTR 1.7%. My real question — how do I lower my CAC? I feel like if I can get CAC down to ₹250 or so the whole thing starts working. What targeting changes would you make?
an0454.assistant:
You're asking how to lower CAC, but CAC isn't what's broken — and chasing it will waste your time. Do the contribution math: ₹850 × 25% − ₹414 = −₹202 per order. You lose ₹202 on every sale. Now suppose you're brilliant and cut CAC from ₹414 all the way to ₹250 — you'd still be at ₹850 × 25% − ₹250 = −₹37 per order. Still underwater. No targeting change on earth fixes that, because the problem isn't the ads.

The disease is your 25% gross margin. At that margin, each order only throws off ₹212 of contribution to cover acquisition — and acquisition almost always costs more than that. You've got a margin problem wearing a marketing costume.

So the lever lives upstream of the ad account: fix the economics first. Pick one — raise prices (haircare can usually take it if positioned right), cut COGS (renegotiate manufacturing, packaging, or per-unit at higher volume), or lift AOV with bundles/subscriptions so each order carries more margin rupees. Get gross margin from 25% toward 45-50% and suddenly a ₹414 CAC is comfortably profitable, no targeting wizardry required.

Caveat: confirm that 25% is true gross margin (COGS + shipping + payment fees), not just COGS — if shipping's buried elsewhere, the hole may be even deeper. Either way, the ads aren't the patient here.

an0457.user: Footwear brand on Meesho Ads, last 30 days post-iOS, spent ₹14L. The Meesho/platform side reports ROAS 4.2 but my Shopify last-click says 1.5. I'm new to this and genuinely confused — which dashboard is telling the truth? How can the same campaign show two numbers this far apart?

Both are "true" from their own angle, and that's exactly why they disagree — the real answer lives between them. The platform's 4.2 is generous: it counts conversions it modelled and gives itself credit for sales it influenced within a click window, even when the buyer didn't come straight back. Shopify's last-click 1.5 is stingy: it only credits whoever got the final tap, so when someone sees your ad, leaves, and returns later via a search or direct visit, the ad gets zero and "direct" gets the medal. One inflates, one deflates. Post-iOS made both worse, because tracking got blurrier.

You'll go in circles trying to pick a winner — they're built to never match. So stop. Anchor on one number neither dashboard can spin: blended CAC. Take your full ₹14L spend, divide by the actual count of new customers Shopify recorded that month. That's what a customer really cost you, end to end, and it doesn't care which platform claims the assist.

Manage to that. If blended CAC sits below your contribution per new customer, the campaign's working regardless of whether the badge says 4.2 or 1.5.

Caveat: blended CAC mixes all your channels together, so once it's your anchor, run an occasional pause-test on Meesho — switch it off for a week and watch whether total orders actually drop. That tells you Meesho's real incremental lift far better than either dashboard.
